item.title: Research on the correlation of artificial intelligence painting tools with adolescents’ art learning motivation and creative effect
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Digital aesthetic education and mental health of children and adolescents are important research topics in the field of public health. The popularity of artificial intelligence painting tools has reshaped the form of art education, but its relationship with adolescents’ art learning motivation, creative self-efficacy and mental health literacy has not yet reached an empirical conclusion. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 342 adolescents assigned to an observation group (AI painting tools, n = 174) and a control group (traditional art tools, n = 168) by prior painting tool use. The Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ), Creative Self-efficacy Scale (ASES), and Mental Health Scale for Chinese Adolescents (MHS-CA) were used for assessment. Propensity scores were estimated via multivariable logistic regression, and stabilized inverse probability weighting (IPTW) balanced baseline demographic, art background and learning frequency covariates; standardized mean differences (SMD) before and after weighting were reported. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) regression explored the nonlinear dose–response relationship between weekly AI painting duration and outcomes. Three knots at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles were chosen based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), with nonlinear p values and 95% CIs of inflection points reported. Multivariate hierarchical covariance analysis, Pearson correlation and Bootstrap mediation models were applied for further analyses. Between-group comparisons were performed on stabilized IPTW-weighted data. Weighted means and robust Huber-White standard errors were calculated. Categorical and continuous variables were compared using the χ 2 test and weighted t -test, respectively. Results After IPTW weighting, the scores of total motivation, intrinsic motivation and creative self-efficacy in the observation group were higher than those in the control group, and the differences between the two groups were statistically significant (t = 6.19, 5.91 and 6.47, all p < 0.001, Cohen’s d was 0.67, 0.64 and 0.70, respectively). Retrospective observation data show that the weekly use time of intelligent painting tools is positively correlated with adolescents’ creative self-efficacy in fine arts (β = 0.462, p < 0.001). The bias-corrected Bootstrap 95% confidence interval shows that there is a significant indirect effect between artistic psychological resilience and aesthetic concentration, and the indirect effect accounts for 41.36% of the total effect. According to the observation data, tool use is related to the lower probability of adolescents’ high art learning burnout (defined by the upper quartile) (OR = 0.429, 95% CI: 0.287–0.642, p < 0.01). Conclusion This retrospective study shows that the use of artificial intelligence painting tools is positively related to adolescents’ art learning motivation and creative self-efficacy, and is related to a low probability of art learning burnout. The above correlation results need to be further verified by prospective cohort study or randomized controlled trial. This study provides a preliminary empirical reference for adolescent digital health aesthetic education, mental health and public health intervention.

item.title: Competency‑based and emotional predictors of pre‑service teachers’ orientation towards the responsible use of Generative AI
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into initial teacher education requires an understanding not only of how frequently these tools are used, but also of the factors that shape their responsible adoption. This study examines how pre‑service teachers’ orientation towards responsible GenAI use is configured, identifying the competency-based resources and usage‑related variables that underpin it, as well as the role of anxiety across the dimensions assessed. A total of 298 pre‑service teachers from two Spanish universities participated, completing a validated 25‑item instrument comprising five dimensions: attitudes towards the use of AI for employability, digital flow in the responsible and safe use of AI, creativity to use AI responsibly, anxiety about using AI in future work contexts, and responsible use of AI for employability. Robust group comparisons, hierarchical regressions, and a network analysis with hierarchical clustering were conducted. The confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the instrument’s five‑factor structure. Creativity (β = 0.42) and digital flow (β = 0.37) emerged as the strongest predictors of responsible use, whereas usage frequency made no unique positive contribution. Anxiety was higher among women and younger participants; in the regression model it was associated with more favourable attitudes and higher digital flow, and with lower creativity only when these were controlled (a suppression effect). It occupied a peripheral position within the correlation network. The findings are synthesised in an exploratory two‑path empirical model that requires confirmatory testing. Initial teacher education may therefore benefit from fostering creative GenAI‑based experiences while deliberately addressing the emotional dimension of learning these technologies.

item.title: Co-Creating Value with Generative AI in Later Life: A Qualitative Diary Study of Older Adults’ Everyday Appropriation
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) presents both opportunities and challenges for later life, with its benefits depending on how older adults appropriate, evaluate, and regulate its use rather than on technical capability alone. Existing research has focused primarily on technology acceptance, offering limited insight into how GenAI becomes valuable after adoption. Drawing on a socio-technical appropriation perspective, this study conducted a 14-day qualitative diary study with 16 community-dwelling older adults to examine everyday GenAI use. Thematic analysis identified four interconnected forms of appropriation: functional, creative, and relational appropriation, which co-created functional, experiential, and relational value; and critical appropriation, which regulated these forms of value while preserving human agency. We propose the GenAI Appropriation and Value Co-creation Framework (GAVC), explaining how older adults transform GenAI into a capability-expanding resource that supports later-life well-being. The framework advances appropriation theory and informs GenAI system design and literacy initiatives that foster active, productive aging.

item.title: Production-source disclosures, higher-order creative attributions, and audience reception of two-dimensional animation: evidence from a randomized source-disclosure experiment
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Attribution theory explains how audiences use observable information to infer otherwise unobservable agents and processes behind creative work. This study applied this perspective to examine how production-source disclosures influence source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience reception of two-dimensional animation. Methods In a randomized experiment, 626 adults were assigned to one of four production-source disclosure conditions—undisclosed, human-made, human–AI collaborative, or AI-led—while viewing the same three animation clips, all of which were actually produced through human–AI collaboration. We examined between-condition differences in source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience-reception outcomes, as well as concurrent associations between higher-order creative attributions and audience reception. Results The disclosures clearly differentiated participants’ perceptions of AI and human involvement. Perceived creative effort was statistically significant before correction but did not meet the α = 0.05 criterion after Holm adjustment ( p = 0.0502); the only corrected contrast indicated lower perceived creative effort in the human–AI collaborative condition than in the human-made condition. No statistically reliable omnibus between-condition differences emerged for perceived authorship, perceived emotional authenticity, artistic evaluation, situational immersion, or viewing and recommendation intention. Higher-order creative attributions were positively associated with all three audience-reception indicators in concurrent analyses, although the strong correlation between perceived emotional authenticity and situational immersion warrants caution about measurement overlap. Discussion The findings indicate that the diagnosticity of a production-source cue depends on the judgment target: the disclosures clearly reorganized perceived production roles but did not yield statistically reliable corresponding differences across most higher-order creative attributions or reception outcomes. The attribution–reception relations represent concurrent covariation rather than causal mediation. Because the three clips were presented in a fixed order, material and order effects cannot be separated, and the equivalence analyses did not establish negligible between-condition differences.

item.title: An interpretable machine learning framework for student depression risk prediction: integrating multi-domain features with SHAP-based explainability
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Depression among university students constitutes a pressing global mental health challenge, with prevalence rates exceeding 30% in numerous populations. While traditional screening instruments such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) offer effective clinical detection, they are inherently reactive and focus solely on symptom assessment, lacking the ability to capture modifiable risk factors. Machine learning (ML) approaches, particularly ensemble methods with explainability frameworks, present a promising avenue for risk stratification using multi-domain data. Objective This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable XGBoost-based prediction model integrating academic, demographic, lifestyle, and clinical features to predict student depression risk, and to systematically evaluate model performance, feature contributions, and clinical utility using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and Decision Curve Analysis (DCA). Methods A cross-sectional dataset of 27,901 student records with 16 multi-domain features was analyzed. XGBoost was trained with 80/20 stratified split (n_train = 22,320, n_test = 5,581). Model performance was assessed via area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration (Brier score), and DCA. Feature importance was quantified through SHAP values, and eight predefined hypotheses concerning risk factor directionality, dose-response relationships, and domain contributions were tested. Results The XGBoost model achieved AUC = 0.919, accuracy = 0.845, F1-score = 0.869, and Brier score = 0.111. The strongest predictors by mean | SHAP| were suicidal ideation (1.212), Academic Pressure (0.934), and Financial Stress (0.679). Financial Stress and Work/Study Hours demonstrated clear monotonic dose-response relationships. CGPA showed significant linear association (R 2 = 0.473, p < 0.001). The multi-domain model significantly outperformed all single-domain models ( p < 0.001). DCA confirmed net clinical benefit across threshold probabilities of 10%–50%. A sensitivity model excluding suicidal ideation maintained good performance (AUC = 0.868), supporting its practical utility in ethically constrained screening contexts. Conclusion The XGBoost + SHAP framework demonstrates robust predictive performance, excellent calibration, and clinically meaningful interpretability for student depression risk assessment. Multi-domain integration is essential for comprehensive risk profiling. These findings support the development of explainable ML-based screening tools for educational mental health settings.

item.title: Who Punishes LLM Alignment? User Characteristics and the Evaluation of Ethical Response Refusals
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Ethical refusals are essential for aligning large language models (LLMs) with safety constraints, yet users often penalize them in comparative evaluations. Whether this refusal penalty varies systematically across users remains unclear. Drawing on human–computer interaction research, we examine how users’ evaluative priorities and usage intensity shape responses to ethical refusals. Using the PRISM alignment dataset, which links LLM evaluations to user characteristics, we find that safety preferences significantly mitigate refusal penalties, whereas preferences for helpfulness, fluency, and creativity do not. Heavy users penalize refusals more strongly, an association substantially mediated by lower safety preferences. These findings suggest that acceptance of safety-aligned behavior depends primarily on users’ safety orientation rather than preferences for instrumental response qualities. Our results highlight the limitations of evaluating LLM safety alignment through aggregate user preferences and underscore the importance of accounting for user heterogeneity in evaluation benchmarks and deployment decisions.

item.title: Exploring characteristics of primary school students’ behaviors and interaction qualities in human-GenAI collaborative creative problem-solving activities
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
Creative problem-solving (CPS) is essential for addressing complex and uncertain problems, yet it is challenging for learners to develop high-quality solutions. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new possibilities for supporting CPS by facilitating divergent and convergent thinking. However, how learners with different performance levels engage in human-GenAI collaborative CPS remains underexplored. This study investigated the CPS processes of 25 students in Grades 4-6. Specifically, descriptive statistics and lag sequential analysis were used to examine students' behavioral characteristics and sequences, respectively, while epistemic network analysis was employed to investigate interaction qualities. The findings indicated that primary school students exhibited more behaviors in the idea generation and solution validation stages, reflecting a task-oriented behavioral pattern supported by GenAI. Significant differences in behavioral sequences across performance levels were observed: high-performing groups (HPGs) demonstrated clearer CPS goals and more continuous, progressive behavioral sequences, whereas low-performing groups (LPGs) showed less defined goals and more fragmented behavioral sequences. In terms of interaction qualities, HPGs were more effective at facilitating CPS through strategic questioning and the productive use of feedback, while LPGs were characterized by more superficial interactions. These findings provided theoretical insights and empirical evidence to inform human-GenAI collaborative CPS in primary education.

item.title: TaleBridge: An AI-Mediated System for Supporting Perspective Taking and Creative Subjectivity in Children’s Asynchronous Collaborative Storytelling
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Intelligent tools for children’s storytelling support idea generation and multimodal expression, yet most prioritize individual creation over peer collaboration. This study investigates how AI can support children’s asynchronous collaborative story writing while preserving their creative subjectivity. Through a formative study, we derived five design goals and developed TaleBridge, an AI-mediated system combining private ideation spaces, shared negotiation mechanisms, AI-generated textual and visual scaffolds, and a reflection module. In a within-subjects user study, we compared the full version with a baseline version retaining asynchronous writing, co-writing, and plot decomposition. Final stories produced with the full version were shorter and contained fewer plot events, while no statistically significant difference in narrative logic ratings was detected between conditions. Expert ratings indicated higher creative subjectivity, and children reported more positive collaborative experiences. TaleBridge’s overall configuration may support children in examining, comparing, and negotiating each other’s narrative intentions, while leaving creative decisions to children.

item.title: How Do Users Organize Prompting Workflows in Human–AI Collaboration? A Process Mining Analysis of AI Literacy-Based Strategy Patterns
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Growing use of large language models (LLMs) in creative and knowledge work has increased interest in how users collaborate with AI beyond output quality. This study examines how AI literacy and task type relate to prompting strategy organization, workflow, and perceptions of collaboration in ChatGPT-supported writing. Forty university students completed a divergent brand-naming and a convergent writing task. Prompting logs were analyzed using sequential pattern metrics and process mining, complemented by interviews. Higher AI literacy was associated with more structured coordination among prompting strategies, whereas lower literacy showed more repetitive, generation-centered pathways. These differences appeared in specific transition and loop configurations rather than overall transition diversity. Participants described AI as assistive, yet behavioral traces showed substantial AI contribution to outputs. These findings provide process-oriented insights into how AI literacy and task type relate to strategic adaptability in human–AI collaboration.

item.title: Design-thinking scaffolds for learner-agency-preserving AI use: effects on creative self-efficacy, cognitive flexibility, and engagement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative AI can facilitate the production of student work but may also displace learners' responsibility for problem framing, evaluation, and revision. This study examined whether design-thinking scaffolds were associated with creative self-efficacy, cognitive flexibility, and problem-solving engagement during AI-supported project learning. Methods A three-condition, four-wave quasi-experimental study included 162 undergraduates in six intact class sections (54 per condition). Non-AI project learning, ordinary GenAI use, and design-thinking-scaffolded GenAI use were compared across a four-week educational design task. Baseline-adjusted models assessed self-reported outcomes, human-coded AI-use logs, and independently rated products from 54 teams. Cluster-bootstrap analyses examined temporally ordered indirect associations and moderation by pre-intervention AI over-reliance. Results Compared with ordinary GenAI, the scaffolded condition showed higher T2 creative self-efficacy (adjusted difference = 0.33, p = 0.006), T3 cognitive flexibility (0.35, p = 0.003), and T4 engagement (0.35, p = 0.004). Mean team product quality was 20.14 in the scaffolded condition, compared with 17.62 under ordinary GenAI and 16.76 without AI. Coded prompts showed fewer answer-completion requests and more comparison, critique, and reflection. Indirect estimates via creative self-efficacy (0.07), cognitive flexibility (0.09), and their sequential pathway (0.04) had bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. Higher initial AI over-reliance weakened the overall engagement contrast and the two single-mediator indirect pathways, whereas the moderated-sequential index had a confidence interval including zero. Discussion The findings are consistent with agency-preserving cognitive offloading when instructional scaffolds retain student responsibility for higher-order decisions. Intact-section allocation, task-specific self-reports, and limited section-level replication preclude strong causal or general-transfer claims.

item.title: Code Craft: the digital design thinking and learning platform to enhance computational thinking and digital literacy
item.description:
Smart Learning Environments
Abstract This research develops an educational platform utilizing a design-thinking model to enhance computational thinking and digital literacy among undergraduate students in Thailand. The study was conducted in three phases: (1) investigating the learning experiences and needs of 400 learners and instructors; (2) designing and developing the integrated design-thinking model to improve computational thinking; and (3) deploying the platform and design-thinking learning model to enhance student computational thinking using 28 undergraduate students, evaluating its effectiveness and learner satisfaction. Quantitative analysis revealed that the platform significantly improved computational thinking mean scores at the 0.05 level, suggesting its potential as an effective learning tool. The prototype learning innovation comprises four key components: (1) fostering computational skills and digital literacy, with an emphasis on logical and algorithmic thinking, data handling, and software usage; (2) online assistance through the learning platform “Code Craft,” providing support and resources; (3) digital and artificial intelligence tools, facilitating interactive, modern learning experiences; and (4) enjoyment, ensuring an engaging and motivating learning process. The steps in this process are as follows: (1) discovering insights into learners’ needs and challenges; (2) tailoring the platform to user requirements; (3) generating ideas, encouraging creativity and innovative thinking; (4) prototyping solutions, developing practical applications and tools; and (5) testing and iteration, refining the platform from feedback and performance data. This approach illustrates the effectiveness of combining design-thinking instructional models and gamification in educational platform development, significantly improving computational thinking, preparing students for the labor market, and addressing the skills gap in technology and computational skills in higher education.

item.title: An Agent-Based Model of GenAI in Creative Writing: Novelty Gains and Diversity Declines
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being rapidly adopted in education. Its effects on creativity unfold at both individual and collective levels. We develop an agent-based model that represents students’ creative outputs in a two-dimensional idea space to examine how GenAI assistance in creative writing shapes individual creativity and classroom-level idea diversity. Simulations show that GenAI increases individual creativity, with disproportionately larger gains for less creative students, while reducing collective diversity through idea homogenization. Critically, the model reveals a more nuanced, non-linear pattern of collective diversity than empirical accounts of homogenization alone: collective diversity can increase at low-to-moderate adoption rates before reaching a tipping point and declining at high adoption rates. These findings highlight the need to evaluate GenAI in education using both individual performance metrics and collective system outcomes.

item.title: Artificial intelligence readiness and innovative work behavior among university engineering teachers: parallel indirect effects of creative self-efficacy and technology integration self-efficacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming part of university teachers’ teaching and research, yet its relationship with innovative work behavior in engineering education remains unclear. Methods Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and Conservation of Resources Theory, this cross-sectional study surveyed 786 university engineering teachers in Chongqing, China. We examined the association between AI readiness and innovative work behavior and tested parallel indirect effects through creative self-efficacy and technology integration self-efficacy. Gender and educational attainment were included as covariates. Results AI readiness was positively associated with innovative work behavior. The indirect paths through creative self-efficacy and technology integration self-efficacy were both significant. AI readiness remained significantly associated with innovative work behavior after both mediators were included, indicating partial mediation. Discussion These findings suggest that AI readiness and efficacy beliefs may support innovative work among engineering teachers. Universities can support quality education by linking AI training to course design, laboratory teaching, project development, and research tasks, while using guided practice and feedback to build teachers’ confidence.

item.title: From Briefing to Prompt: How Users Translate Textual Design Instructions into Text-to-Image Prompts
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Text-to-image systems support creative, educational, and professional work, yet how users translate briefs into effective prompts remains underexplored. This study examines prompt formulation and refinement by 23 participants using ChatGPT with DALL·E 3 under two task configurations: low-detail briefings with multiple reformulations and high-detail briefings with one reformulation. A structured literature review and qualitative analysis of 81 prompts, 81 images, interviews, and observation notes, supported by inter-coder agreement, identified recurring strategies, difficulties expressing visual intentions, and refinement patterns. High-detail/single-reformulation tasks produced semantically denser prompts and closer alignment with intended outcomes; low-detail/multiple-reformulation tasks encouraged exploratory prompting and interpretive variation. Because briefing detail and reformulation opportunities varied together, these findings reflect task-configuration differences, not isolated effects of briefing complexity. Framing prompting as cognitive and creative mediation in human–AI interaction, the study proposes a process model spanning briefing interpretation, semantic extraction, visual attribute selection, prompt structuring, generation, and refinement, requiring further validation.

item.title: Academic Pressures, Generative AI Use, and Academic Behaviors and Perceptions Among University Students: An Empirical Study
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
This study draws on cognitive offloading theory and self-regulated learning theory to investigate why Chinese university students use Generative AI (GenAI) and what academic correlates are observed. Using a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 500 university students and analyzed through structural equation modeling (SEM) and bootstrap mediation analysis. The results show that academic workload, time pressure, and sensitivity to grades are positively associated with GenAI usage, whereas sensitivity to quality is not. In addition, GenAI usage is positively associated with procrastination and self-reported memory difficulties. Regarding the competing hypotheses on creative engagement, GenAI usage was positively associated with creative engagement, which may indicate that students may use GenAI for ideation rather than answer retrieval. Mediation analyses confirm that GenAI usage significantly mediates the associations between academic workload, time pressure, sensitivity to grades, and the three outcomes. However, the indirect effects of sensitivity to quality on the three outcomes were not significant, consistent with the unsupported hypothesis. The study highlights the need to strengthen students’ AI literacy training, manage academic workload, and redesign assessment methods so as to balance responsible use with academic integrity. Future research should employ longitudinal designs, multi-method measures, and explore these relationships in diverse educational contexts to gain a more comprehensive understanding.

item.title: Same Stimulus, Different Ideas: Prior Knowledge and the Integration of AI-Generated Stimuli in Creative Ideation
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
External stimuli can expand the conceptual space during creative ideation, yet individuals may incorporate the same stimuli differently depending on the knowledge and experience available to them. This issue bears on the information-processing mechanisms of creativity and on the use of generative artificial intelligence as a source of stimuli. Nine groups (221 participants) from three educational and sociocultural contexts (Indigenous and Afro-descendant community members holding traditional knowledge, rural school students, and university students) took part in ideation workshops to design agro-industrial products. Stimuli were generated with a large language model. Semantic and conceptual embedding similarity and topic modelling were used to compare initial ideas, stimuli, and final ideas. Topic models of these very short texts were unstable. In the community and school groups, conceptual integration generally stayed close to the initial proximity between ideas and stimuli, whereas the university groups more often exceeded it, a tendency that held across alternative representations but not in every group. Coffee-domain groups, whose ideas and stimuli shared the vocabulary of the raw material, combined high persistence with high integration. Three exploratory forms of integration are proposed: conceptual reinterpretation, expansion, and transformation. The analyses are descriptive, and prior knowledge was not measured directly.

item.title: Value of a Human Mind: How Perceived AI-Authorship Shapes Willingness to Pay for Cultural Goods
item.description:
Creativity Research Journal
Artificial intelligence is increasingly involved in the production of cultural goods, raising important questions about how consumers evaluate creativity. This research examines how perceived authorship, whether a work is believed to be created by a human or by artificial intelligence, shapes willingness to pay. Across five experiments, we manipulate the attributed origin of artworks while holding the visual stimulus constant, isolating the psychological consequences of authorship beliefs rather than objective production differences. Results reveal a robust preference for works believed to be human-created. This effect is driven primarily by lower perceived authenticity and emotional sensitivity attributed to AI creators. Egocentrism further moderates the relationship, such that consumers lower in egocentrism exhibit stronger preferences for human authorship. Two predicted boundary conditions, the expressive purpose of the artwork and framing AI as a creative tool, did not significantly alter the effect, suggesting that the perceived presence of a human mind serves as a powerful signal in consumer valuation. These findings advance current understanding of how perceived authorship influences the value of cultural goods and contribute to broader theories of creativity by highlighting the enduring psychological importance of human agency in artistic contexts. Practical implications extend to creators, marketers, and platforms, navigating the integration of AI into cultural production.

item.title: Generative AI configurations across creative phases: a 2 × 2 experiment on creative performance and immediate knowledge in art and design education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in art and design education, but it remains unclear whether text-based and image-generative configurations offer different advantages across creative phases or whether sequencing them improves final outcomes. Methods In a randomized 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment, 120 art and design students (30 per condition) completed a standardized cultural-heritage chromatic reconstruction task. Participants were assigned to Text-to-Text, Text-to-Image, Image-to-Text, or Image-to-Image configurations across divergent exploration and convergent development. Expert-rated creative performance, immediate task-relevant knowledge, and human–AI interaction processes were assessed. The four primary hypothesis tests were evaluated with Holm correction. Results Text-based AI during divergence produced higher divergent creative performance than image-generative AI (mean difference = 0.823, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Image-generative AI during convergence yielded higher Aesthetic Quality at the unadjusted level (difference = 0.493, p = 0.026), but not after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.052). The hypothesized Text-to-Image sequence did not significantly outperform alternatives in Overall Creative Performance (contrast = 0.066, p = 0.671), and the factorial interaction was nonsignificant ( p = 0.541). However, Text-to-Image achieved higher baseline-adjusted immediate post-task knowledge scores (contrast = 1.478, 95% CI [1.050, 1.906], p < 0.001), without a significant cross-phase interaction ( p = 0.404). Discussion GenAI configuration effects differed across creative phases and outcomes, but phase-specific advantages did not establish a superior final creative-product sequence. Because AI modality was bundled with interaction and interface characteristics, and the knowledge assessments had limited reliability, the results do not establish isolated modality effects, durable learning, or synergistic sequencing. AI orchestration should remain a provisional, context-sensitive instructional perspective requiring further validation.

item.title: Extension-semantic prompting for AI-generated traditional Chinese patterns: behavioral and semantic-aesthetic evaluation with exploratory fNIRS analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background This study developed the Extension-Semantic Prompting Framework (ESPF) to organize cultural-semantic information in prompts for AI-generated traditional Chinese patterns. The framework decomposes traditional patterns into seven semantic-aesthetic dimensions and maps them onto structured prompt slots and corresponding evaluation items. Methods The experiment included 18 experts and 18 laypeople as participants. Stimuli comprised images of five traditional pattern themes generated using Stable Diffusion and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) models under the ESPF and Free conditions. Liking ratings, response times (RTs), and semantic-aesthetic questionnaire responses were analyzed using cross-classified mixed-effects models, while prefrontal functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data were examined using region-of-interest (ROI) and general linear model analyses. Results Mixed-effects analyses showed that the ESPF condition was associated with shorter aesthetic-judgment RTs and higher framework-derived semantic-aesthetic ratings, although the latter varied significantly across pattern themes. Interpretation of the RT difference is limited by the fixed Free–ESPF presentation order. The overall condition effect on liking was not significant after accounting for participant and image variability. No stable condition-related effect was observed in the prefrontal ROIs, and exploratory between-group neural differences were not robust across adjusted and GLM analyses. Conclusion ESPF provides a structured approach to organizing cultural semantics in AI-generated traditional patterns. The selective differences observed across evaluation outcomes and pattern themes highlight the need to balance semantic control with creative openness in prompt-supported human–AI collaborative design.

item.title: Humanlike Self-Enhancement and Self-Protection in Generative Pre-Trained Transformer-Based AI Agents: Of Overclaiming and the Self-Serving Bias
item.description:
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
We investigated whether GPT-based AI agents, despite presumably lacking humanlike sentience, emulate motivated behavior in group settings. We focused on overclaiming (overestimating one’s contribution to group outcomes) and the self-serving bias (taking disproportionate credit for group successes while deflecting blame for group failures). We conducted eight experiments involving a collaborative and creative group task (joke-writing). AI agents consistently overclaimed their own contributions. An egocentrism-reduction manipulation (directing attention equally to one’s own and others’ contributions) attenuated, but did not eliminate, overclaiming. Further, AI agents exhibited the self-serving bias. Overclaiming persisted across variations in temperature settings and demographic personas (gender, ethnicity), and was more pronounced in later GPT models. Chain-of-Thought reasoning did not reduce, and instead increased, overclaiming. AI systems can mimic human self-enhancement and self-protection, raising implications for the emergence of motivated self-like behavior in non-biological systems, the assumed neutrality of LLMs, and the need for improved mitigation techniques.

item.title: Hybrid Human-AI Creativity: Navigating the Affordance Landscape of Creative Exploration
item.description:
Creativity Research Journal
The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems capable of producing text, images, music, and design artifacts has intensified debates about the nature of creativity and the locus of creative agency. Current discussions often frame these technologies either as replacing human creativity or as merely augmenting human creative processes. Such perspectives remain theoretically limited because they conceptualize creativity primarily as an individual cognitive ability rather than a distributed process embedded within sociocultural and material environments. Drawing on ecological approaches to cognition and contemporary creativity research, this paper proposes a conceptual framework that reconceptualizes human-AI creativity as navigation within an expanded affordance landscape. Integrating classical creativity process models with sociocultural and distributed perspectives, GenAI systems are conceptualized as affordance-modulating artifacts that reshape the topology of creative exploration. The framework explains how generative systems expand ideational possibility through rapid combinatorial generation while also influencing creative trajectories through algorithmic anchoring. Eight theoretical propositions link AI-mediated affordances to stages of the creative process. The paper extends distributed creativity theory to technologically mediated environments and outlines a research agenda for empirically investigating hybrid human-AI creativity systems.
